learning: If line_loss_events fall and slalom progress rises above 0.18 while the s-bend holds near 0.49, keep the 0.016 m footprint and test wheel_radius next. If the s-bend drops below about 0.45, the blurred edge is costing turn response, so revert to 0.012 m and test wheel_radius with the smaller footprint. If the slalom stays at 0.17 to 0.18 in both cases, the limit is speed or lag, not sensing.
notes: Controller is identical to iteration 4 so that the only change in the race is sensor_size 0.012 to 0.016 m. The Builder's array, wheel_track 0.09 m and mass are kept as proposed. I expect fewer line-loss events and possibly a higher slalom plateau, with the s-bend the main risk.
rationale: Evidence: iteration 4 (score 404.6, best) ran the 5-sensor row at y=0.08 m, 0.012 m footprint, wheel_track 0.09 m, with the controller now used unchanged here (base_speed 1.7, kp 2.5, ki 0.05, kd 0.4, weights -2 to +2, last_direction). It finished 20 of 20 oval runs, with steering_oscillation 0.205 and s-bend progress 0.486. Its slalom progress was 0.177 and s-bend and slalom still ended at max_error about 0.062 to 0.063, with line_loss_events of 1.0 per run on both. Iteration 5 showed that wheel_track 0.08 m cut s-bend progress to 0.330, so 0.09 m is kept. Slalom progress has sat at 0.16 to 0.18 across iterations 1, 3, 4 and 5 whatever the track width or row position, so it is not a turn-authority problem. The Builder's one change is sensor_size from 0.012 to 0.016 m, the largest allowed footprint. A larger footprint covers more of the 25 mm tape at each sensor, which may reduce line-loss dropouts at bend entries. Because the signal is a reading-weighted average, the larger footprint should not change its scale, so I keep the weights and every controller gain unchanged. That isolates the footprint effect against iteration 4. Expected result: line_loss_events below 0.95 per run, slalom progress above 0.18 if sensing was the limit, and s-bend progress held near 0.49. The risk is that a blurred edge costs the s-bend, which is the first thing to check.
